title: Communication is an ecosystem, not a device.
summary: A practical, evidence-informed field guide to multimodal communication: speech, gestures, signs, gaze, objects, photos, AAC, typing, scanning, low-tech backups, communication partners, and using what is already around you.
search: The Communication Field Guide · Updated October 2026 Communication is an ecosystem, not a device. A word. A look toward the door. A familiar gesture. The actual cereal box. A photograph on a phone. A symbol. A typed sentence. A speech-generating device. A switch. A sound. More than one of these, in the same hour. Multimodal communication means keeping enough reliable routes open that a person can say what they mean in the place, body, energy level, and moment they are actually in. Make a communication cardUse what is around you → Evidence and links checked October 3, 2026. This is practical family guidance, not an individualized AAC evaluation. Field note no. 01The best route is the one that works now.The polished answer is not always the useful one. Sometimes the right communication tool is sophisticated technology. Sometimes it is the photograph you took in the parking lot thirty seconds ago. Prestige is not the point. Being understood is. In this guideThe whole toolboxUse what is around youPartner skillPrimary + backupReal-life settingsAI as drafting helpCommunication belongs to the personSources 01 / The whole toolbox There is no prize for using only one route. Augmentative and alternative communication is broader than a particular app or device. ASHA describes AAC as multimodal: people may combine speech or vocalizations, gestures, signs, facial expression, body movement, objects, photographs, visual supports, writing, text, symbols, communication boards or books, speech-generating technology, and different access methods. The mix can change with context, audience, purpose, motor access, fatigue, and sensory conditions. A good system therefore asks two questions at once: What does this person have to say? and what is the easiest reliable route for saying it right now? AaSpeech + vocalizationWords, approximations, sounds, laughter, intonation, and other intentional vocal signals. ✋Gesture + signPointing, reaching, conventional gestures, manual signs, and familiar movements. ◉Gaze + bodyEye gaze, facial expression, orientation, movement, and established body signals that can be confirmed. ●Real objectsThe actual cup, shoe, snack, ticket, towel, or item in front of you can make a choice concrete immediately. ▧Photos + visual scenesCamera-roll pictures, venue photos, screenshots, visual schedules, maps, and pictures of real choices. ✎Drawing + writingSketching, handwriting, note apps, typing, texting, saved phrases, and text-to-speech. ▦Symbols + low-tech AACSymbol displays, communication books, printed backups, and small situation-specific boards alongside robust language. ▣Speech-generating technologyDedicated devices, tablets, and phones with robust symbol- or text-based communication systems. ↳Switch + scanning accessDirect or indirect access that lets a communicator select from available choices using an established signal. The field ruleDo not make speech the tollbooth.Speech is one route. It should not be the price of admission to choice, attention, participation, humor, refusal, privacy, or an ordinary conversation. More than requesting A full communication life includes asking, refusing, commenting, complaining, joking, greeting, telling news, correcting someone, asking questions, changing the subject, seeking help, saying “not that,” and ending the conversation. A system that can only produce “I want” is carrying far too little of the person’s life. Behavior can tell you that something changed. It cannot safely tell you the whole sentence. Pacing, movement, vocalization, withdrawal, reaching, or a facial change may tell a familiar person that something is different. Treat that as information worth responding to, not as permission to assign a precise meaning. “Something seems different—can we figure it out?” plus an accessible way to answer protects agency better than deciding what the person meant. 02 / The useful art of improvising Use what is already around you. Communication does not stop because the perfect material is in another room. Real objects, signs, menus, packaging, maps, tickets, photos, screenshots, timers, calendars, a notes app, a dry-erase board, and the environment itself can all make a message easier to understand or express. These are additions and backups—not reasons to take away a person’s established AAC. At a caféUse the actual menu.Point to categories. Show the picture of the soup. Compare two real items. Let a person point, type, use their device, gesture, or say “none of these.” Keep food choice, size, drink, and “finished” as separate decisions. At the grocery storeThe shelf is already a visual display.Hold up two packages. Point to the cart. Use a saved photo of the familiar brand. Photograph a new item so it can be talked about later. The real object often carries more information than an abstract placeholder. On an outingPhotograph the next step.Take a picture of the entrance, the ticket booth, the pool door, the car, or the bench where a break can happen. A phone camera can turn an unfamiliar sequence into a concrete one in under a minute. At homeLet the house do some of the talking.Use the actual cereal box, bath towel, shoes, calendar, timer, laundry basket, or remote. Pair words and AAC with objects already attached to the routine. In a medical officeMake the invisible visible.A body diagram, mirror, photo, typed note, or showing the relevant body area can reduce language load. Prepare words such as stop, break, hurts, not sure, explain again, and where. Online or in a groupUse the side doors.Chat, advance questions, a shared document, typed responses, and a follow-up message can make participation possible when real-time turn-taking is too fast. A communication tool already in the room still counts. The aim is not to create a Pinterest-perfect support system. The aim is to make meaning easier to send and receive without taking control away from the communicator. The camera roll is a surprisingly good communication drawer. Photos can set a topic, show a person or place, represent a choice, clarify which item someone means, prepare for a visit, or help recall what happened. Use current, meaningful pictures where possible. A photograph of the actual pool is often more useful than a generic blue square labeled “swim.” Visual supports can explain what language alone leaves fuzzy. A short sequence can show where we are going, what happens first, what happens next, where a break can happen, and how we get home. Keep the sequence flexible enough for real life. If something changes, show the change rather than pretending the original plan is still true. 03 / The person across the table matters too The communication partner is part of the system. Research on AAC partner instruction repeatedly points to partner behavior as consequential. The device can be charged, the vocabulary can be excellent, and communication can still collapse if the people nearby rush, quiz, answer for the communicator, or only notice conventional speech. Speak to the person.Ask the communicator the question. A supporter can help with access or context without becoming the person being addressed. Wait longer than feels natural.Looking, motor planning, navigating vocabulary, composing, or switching routes takes time. Silence is not an emergency. Model, do not quiz.Use the communication system while you talk when appropriate. Demonstrate language without turning every interaction into a test. Make “no” work.Offer choices that can genuinely be refused. Include stop, break, finished, not sure, and something else. Respond to credible attempts.A word, look, gesture, device selection, typed message, or established signal deserves a response even when the answer to the request is no. Repair honestly.“I think I missed that. Can we try another way?” is better than pretending to understand. Do not move communication out of reach.Ask before touching or relocating a personal communication device. Communication access should not be treated as a reward. Check the environment.Noise, glare, seating, positioning, battery, volume, Wi-Fi, visual clutter, and fatigue can all make a familiar route much harder. Field note no. 02Partner skill can lower the effort of being understood.Good support does not make the message for the person. It makes room, time, access, and another route when the first one is difficult. 04 / Redundancy is civilized Choose a primary route and a backup before you need the backup. Electronics lose power. Sunlight makes screens hard to see. Pools are wet. Restaurants are loud. Motor access can change with fatigue. A familiar staff member is absent. Planning two workable routes ahead of time keeps an ordinary problem from becoming a communication emergency. YESNOSTOPBREAKHELPFINISHEDNOT SURESOMETHING ELSE Before leaving the house The person’s primary communication tools are charged, mounted, packed, or otherwise available. A low-tech or lower-effort backup covers the urgent messages that matter in this setting. At least one adult knows the person’s reliable yes/no or selection signals. Situation-specific words have been added without taking away access to the rest of the person’s language. There is a plan for water, glare, noise, a dead battery, a broken mount, or a device that suddenly refuses to cooperate. The person can refuse, change course, and end the activity—not only request it. Turn this into a field card ASHA guidance supports ongoing access to AAC and multiple modalities; concerns about ordinary recreational “screen time” do not apply to a screen being used for communication. 05 / Ordinary places, different demands Build the route around the setting. PoolKeep the device dry. Keep communication wet-proof.A waterproof or laminated backup can cover stop, more, out, bathroom, cold, help, finished, and something else. Establish how yes/no will work in the water. Keep the full system nearby in a safe dry place. RestaurantA menu is both language and clutter.Use the actual menu, photos, pointing, text, or a short display. Separate the decisions: entrée, side, cup or glass, more, finished. Keep “none of these” available. School or programConsistency is not sameness.Keep core language and access available across rooms and people. A brief communication profile, charging plan, backup, and access notes make the system less dependent on one familiar adult. Medical visitThe historian should not replace the patient.Ask the person first when possible. A supporter can clarify history and access while still leaving room for the patient’s own yes/no, stop, pain, fear, not sure, and questions. High stressLower effort, not expectations of personhood.Stress may make a usual communication route harder. Offer a familiar lower-effort route, reduce competing sensory demands, wait, and keep urgent messages easy to reach. New peoplePut the interaction rules on one small card.“Please speak directly to me. I communicate using [routes]. Give me about [time] to answer. If that route is hard, try [backup]. Please do not [ ].” 06 / AI can do the clerical work Let AI format the support. Do not let it invent the person. AI can be genuinely useful for turning known facts into a clean card, simplifying a venue’s information, organizing a visual sequence, formatting current choices, creating a plain-language version, or drafting a handoff. The safe dividing line is authorship: the tool may help organize and present information; it should not claim to know what the person thinks, wants, understands, or feels. Good useTurn real facts into a visual plan.Give the AI the actual location, sequence, photos or descriptions, break option, and way home. Ask for a short plan using only those facts. Good useMake current choices easier to scan.Paste today’s actual menu or activity choices. Ask the AI to group them clearly without adding unavailable options. Good useProduce two reading levels.Keep the meaning the same while asking for a compact card and a fuller staff note. The details stay consistent; the presentation changes. Good useTranslate a known message.Translation can help bridge languages. Preserve the original alongside the translation when precision matters and verify important wording. Do notAsk AI to read someone’s mind.Do not turn a photo, behavior, movement, or supporter’s hunch into a claimed statement of what the person wants or feels. Do notUpload private history because the prompt has an empty box.Use the minimum information needed for the communication task. A restaurant host does not need a medical chart to wait fifteen seconds for an answer. Free shared toolThe Communication Card MakerEnter the routes, yes/no signals, wait time, backup, and practical notes. It creates a printable field card, a one-page profile, and a reusable AI prompt.Open the generator → 07 / Agency first Communication belongs to the person. Support can make access easier without taking over the message. The aim is not for a partner to become a better guesser. The aim is for the communicator to have reliable ways to initiate, choose, refuse, clarify, disagree, repair, and end an interaction. Final selections stay with the communicator.Suggestions, prediction, modeling, or visual organization can reduce effort. The person still chooses the message. Interpretation is labeled as interpretation.If a supporter thinks a behavior may mean discomfort, say “I wonder if…” and seek confirmation rather than presenting the guess as the person’s statement. Unexpected answers are allowed.A communication system should make it possible to disagree with the supporter, pick the option nobody predicted, or introduce a new topic. Repair is shared work.When meaning is unclear, both people can slow down, change route, add context, and try again. Field note no. 03Presume a right to communicate, not a message you have already decided.Respect means access, time, useful language, and the freedom to surprise the person who thought they knew the answer. 08 / Sources + further reading Where this field guide is grounded. ASHA Practice Portal: Augmentative and Alternative CommunicationClinical overview of multimodal AAC, no-prerequisite access, selection techniques, partner training, intervention, and ongoing adaptation. CommunicationFIRST: Communicating in Times of StressPractical guidance on changing communication access under stress, using multiple routes, and preparing a short information page. CommunicationFIRST: Best Practices for Online Meetings with AAC UsersAdvance questions, adequate response time, chat and asynchronous participation, and avoiding interruption while someone composes a message. AssistiveWare: Planning for communication when AAC is not availablePractical multimodal backups using gestures, photos, real objects, writing, environmental clues, and low-tech supports. Individualized assistive and communication technology review (2026)A current look at emerging access technologies and the importance of individualized usability. The evidence base and technology change. The practical principles here are deliberately separated from individualized clinical recommendations. For a person-specific AAC assessment, involve appropriately qualified professionals and the communicator themselves. Take the useful part with youMake a card. Print it. Copy it. Use it with AI.The free generator turns the details that matter into something another person can actually use in the next ten minutes.Make a communication card →

title: One good plan. Room to enjoy it.
summary: The pretty part is easy to find. These are the details that help a family day out or a weekend away actually work: beds, food, water, waiting, and somewhere to pause.
search: Field notes · New England weekendsOne good plan. Room to enjoy it.The pretty part is easy to find. These are the details that help a family day out or a weekend away actually work: beds, food, water, waiting, and somewhere to pause.From our family notebook · New England weekendsThe weekends we remember best are usually the ones we did not overfill.We went north with the usual collection of things that makes a family weekend possible: more chargers than people, swim things, familiar food, one bag that had somehow become the bag for everything, and a plan that looked considerably shorter than the plans we used to make. That last part turned out to be the important one.Maine did not need much help from us. We had a room in Wells where the indoor pool could be the event instead of the reward after a day of sightseeing. We could unpack enough to know where the important things were, swim, come back, eat something easy and decide what—if anything—we wanted to do next. A hotel is much more useful to us when it behaves like a small home base than when it behaves like a glamorous place we are afraid to muss up.Freeport worked the same way. Once we stopped treating the whole town as a shopping assignment, L.L.Bean became its own outing: the giant boot, the fish, a wander through things made for weather, one or two things actually worth looking for, and then out. Kennebunk gave us ice cream that felt like an event without taking over the afternoon. Kittery gave us the very glamorous combination of affordable food in a bag and a gorgeous old fort by the water, which may be one of the most efficient ways to feel as though you have properly gone to Maine.None of these moments was enormous. That is the point. We have become collectors of small, repeatable family pleasures: the pool you can go back to twice, the bookstore where everybody can wander at a different speed, the coastal view you can enjoy without first walking three miles, the familiar meal that prevents the beautiful part of the day from collapsing under hunger.So this section of An AUsome Life is not really about “doing New England.” It is about finding the version of New England that still feels good when everybody is actually there. One good thing. A little room around it. The practical details left in. And enough energy at the end to remember the day fondly instead of merely surviving the itinerary.From our family camera roll · Maine.Family story, lightly edited from our notes, memory and camera roll. title: Their interests. Their choices. The help they need.
summary: An older teen can need substantial support and still want a say in clothes, activities and everyday life. Begin with the person, then make the practical details work around them.
search: The older-teen editTheir interests. Their choices. The help they need.An older teen can need substantial support and still want a say in clothes, activities and everyday life. Begin with the person, then make the practical details work around them.In this guideStart with a real interest.Find a part worth taking part in.Shop for access in the details.A real part in a useful project.Choose photographs for a small photo gift, help choose a gift-kit project, or make a day-plan card using familiar communication and support. Start with a real interest. Swimming, music, food, a favorite film, being outside: an activity has a better starting point when there is something the person enjoys in it. Ask in the way they communicate, allow time, and pay attention to their response. Familiar preferences can help you offer possibilities without deciding everything for them. Keep the choices real. If there is time for either a short walk or a visit to the pool, offer those. A long list of unavailable activities makes the decision harder for everyone. Show the actual item or place when that is useful.Break a large choice into smaller ones: activity first, then time or what to bring.Include a way to say “no,” “something else,” “break” or “finished.”Use the person's established communication methods and usual support. Age-respectful does not mean policing someone's taste. A much-loved character, toy or familiar activity can remain a genuine favorite. Present choices respectfully and let the person enjoy what they enjoy. Find a part worth taking part in. Look at an everyday activity and separate the pieces. For assembling a gift, someone could choose the item, select the paper, place it in a bag or decide which ribbon to use. For an outing, they could choose the destination or the music for the journey. Prepare the parts that would otherwise get in the way, using the support the person ordinarily has. Keep their chosen role meaningful. If they select the blue paper, use the blue paper. Their contribution should affect what happens. Before you begin Put the materials within comfortable reach and keep the workspace clear.Explain or show what is happening in a familiar way.Check whether the tools, closures and instructions are manageable with the usual assistance.Leave enough time for a response before adding another instruction.Make a pause or an early finish possible. A first try can be brief. Watching, choosing, doing one part or returning another day are all possible ways to join in. Offer assistance without making independence the price of participation, and let a refusal remain a refusal. Shop for access in the details. Before buying an activity or product, trace the steps between opening it and enjoying it. Does it require reading, precise timing, several tiny pieces or repeated setup? Can it be restarted easily? Is the enjoyable part accessible with the support already available? Clothes, accessories and everyday equipment Consider the wearer's preferred look alongside fabric, fit and fastenings. For a bag or device accessory, check actual dimensions, weight, access to controls and how it will be carried. A long feature list tells you very little about an awkward zip. Plans outside the house Ask about group size, noise, waiting, facilities and whether the usual support person can join. Find out what a shorter visit would involve and where a break can happen. A clear description or a few current photographs may help make the plan familiar. Keep personal information private when arranging support. Share the access details the host needs, and discuss photos separately rather than assuming participation includes being photographed. Afterward, consider what the teen seemed to enjoy and ask for their view in an accessible way. Keep the useful parts and adjust the awkward ones. A good activity leaves room for both help and personal choice.
